title: Ecuador's Banana Export Boom Begins
description: Ecuador entered the global banana market as a major supplier, overtaking Central American producers affected by Panama disease. Within a decade Ecuador became the world's leading banana exporter, fundamentally reshaping its economy and rural labor patterns. President Galo Plaza's agricultural credits, port investment, and road construction drove the rapid ascent.

title: Ecuador Declares 200-Mile Maritime Zone (Declaration of Santiago)
description: Ecuador, alongside Chile and Peru, signed the Declaration of Santiago asserting a 200-nautical-mile maritime zone — a pioneering document that presaged modern international maritime law. Ecuador subsequently seized US fishing vessels operating within the zone, triggering the 'Tuna Wars' and straining bilateral relations for decades.

title: Velasco Ibarra Wins Third Presidential Term
description: Populist leader José María Velasco Ibarra won the presidency for the third time, riding a wave of popular discontent with elite-dominated politics. His mercurial leadership style and inability to build legislative coalitions would destabilize his tenure and foreshadow yet another military intervention.

title: Military Coup Ousts Velasco Ibarra
description: President Velasco Ibarra was removed from office by a military coup, marking another interrupted term for the populist leader. The coup reflected deep institutional tensions between civilian populism and military conservatism, establishing a recurring pattern in Ecuadorian politics.

title: Ecuador Solidifies Position as World's Largest Banana Exporter
description: Ecuador accounted for approximately 25% of global banana trade, transforming rural labor markets and drawing thousands of internal migrants to coastal plantation regions. The achievement reinforced the country's economic dependence on a single commodity and established a 'banana republic' dynamic despite domestic producer ownership.

title: Galapagos Islands Declared National Park
description: Ecuador officially declared the Galapagos Islands a national park, protecting 97% of the archipelago's land area from development and institutionalizing global conservation through the Charles Darwin Research Station. The designation began a conservation legacy for islands made famous by Darwin's evolutionary research.

title: Velasco Ibarra Wins Fourth Term; Ecuador Breaks with Cuba
description: José María Velasco Ibarra was elected president for the fourth time on a populist platform, but under US pressure severed diplomatic relations with Cuba following the OAS resolution on hemispheric security. The decision deepened divisions between Ecuador's left and the pro-US establishment during a pivotal Cold War moment.

title: Military Junta Overthrows President Arosemena
description: A four-man military junta overthrew President Carlos Julio Arosemena, citing his perceived leftist sympathies, initiating a period of direct military governance from 1963 to 1966. The coup reflected Cold War anti-communism and ended civilian rule during a critical period of social transformation.

title: Military Junta Abolishes Huasipungo and Enacts Agrarian Reform
description: The military junta abolished the huasipungo — a form of unfree indigenous labor tied to hacienda estates persisting since colonial times — and promulgated Ecuador's first Agrarian Reform Law. The reform freed tens of thousands of indigenous Andean workers from debt peonage, though land redistribution remained weak and underfunded.

title: Amazon Territory Opened for Oil Exploration
description: The military government opened the Ecuadorian Amazon (Oriente) to international oil exploration, granting Texaco-Gulf a major concession that set in motion decades of extraction and environmental damage. This single decision would transform Ecuador's fiscal landscape and trigger some of the most consequential environmental litigation in history.

title: Military Junta Collapses; Return to Civilian Rule
description: Widespread popular protests and elite dissatisfaction forced the military junta to hand power to a civilian provisional government, beginning a transition back toward constitutional democracy. A constituent assembly was convened and Otto Arosemena Gómez designated as interim president pending general elections.

title: Texaco-Gulf Confirms Major Amazon Oil Discovery
description: Texaco and Gulf Oil confirmed major commercial oil discoveries in the Lago Agrio area of the Ecuadorian Amazon, transforming the country's economic prospects and setting the stage for the 1972 oil boom. A new constitution was also adopted this year establishing the democratic framework for the following decade.

title: Velasco Ibarra Wins Fifth and Final Presidential Term
description: José María Velasco Ibarra was elected president for the fifth time — an unprecedented achievement in Ecuadorian political history. Facing congressional obstruction and fiscal crisis, he dissolved the legislature and assumed dictatorial powers in 1970, but would ultimately be removed by a military coup in 1972.

title: Ecuador Joins the Andean Pact (Cartagena Agreement)
description: Ecuador joined the Andean Pact alongside Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, and Chile, creating a regional economic integration bloc aimed at fostering industrial development and reducing dependence on extraregional markets. Membership provided a framework for managed trade opening and collective bargaining with multinationals.

title: Military Coup Brings Rodríguez Lara to Power; Oil Exports Begin
description: General Guillermo Rodríguez Lara overthrew President Velasco Ibarra and inaugurated Ecuador's oil era by opening the trans-Andean SOTE pipeline and joining OPEC, earning unprecedented foreign exchange revenues. The coup initiated Ecuador's most transformative decade, as oil revenues funded dramatic state expansion and social programs.

title: CEPE State Oil Company Created
description: Ecuador founded the Corporación Estatal Petrolera Ecuatoriana (CEPE) to manage state participation in the oil sector, renegotiating Texaco-Gulf concession terms and later acquiring a 62.5% stake in the oil consortium. CEPE — later renamed Petroecuador — became the institutional embodiment of Ecuador's resource nationalism.

title: Oil Price Shock Fuels State Expansion and Debt Accumulation
description: The Arab oil embargo quadrupled world oil prices, multiplying Ecuador's oil revenues and funding dramatic expansion of state enterprises, public employment, and import-substitution industries. The government simultaneously began borrowing heavily on international capital markets using oil reserves as collateral — sowing seeds of the 1980s debt crisis.

title: Ecuador Withdraws from OPEC; Failed Counter-Coup Against Rodríguez Lara
description: Ecuador suspended its OPEC membership, citing dissatisfaction with production quotas, while a military faction mounted an unsuccessful coup against General Rodríguez Lara, reflecting divisions within the armed forces over the pace of reform. The weakened government accelerated elite planning for a democratic transition.

title: Military Triumvirate Pledges Democratic Transition
description: A military triumvirate, the Supreme Council of Government, replaced General Rodríguez Lara and committed to a formal transition calendar including a constitutional referendum and presidential elections by 1979. The council's roadmap responded to growing civilian pressure for an end to military rule.

title: Aztra Sugar Mill Massacre
description: Police and military forces suppressed a workers' strike at the Aztra sugar mill in Cañar province, killing scores of workers in one of Ecuador's worst labor massacres. The incident shocked the country and energized the labor movement's demands for democracy and worker rights.

title: 1978 Constitution Grants Illiterates Right to Vote
description: Ecuadorian voters approved a new constitution granting voting rights to the country's large illiterate population for the first time, fundamentally transforming the electorate and enfranchising millions of indigenous and poor citizens. The reform had the greatest impact among indigenous Andean communities previously excluded from formal political participation.

title: Jaime Roldós Elected; Return to Constitutional Democracy
description: Jaime Roldós Aguilera won Ecuador's presidential runoff with a large majority, becoming the first civilian president in a fully democratic Ecuador and marking the formal end of the long military-rule era. His administration launched literacy campaigns, rural development programs, and an independent human rights-centered foreign policy.

title: President Roldós Dies in Plane Crash; Paquisha Conflict with Peru
description: President Jaime Roldós died in a mysterious plane crash on May 24, 1981, with Vice President Osvaldo Hurtado constitutionally assuming the presidency. That same year, Ecuadorian and Peruvian forces clashed in the Paquisha area in a brief border conflict, reigniting nationalist sentiment over the disputed Amazon frontier.

title: Latin American Debt Crisis and IMF Structural Adjustment
description: The regional debt crisis triggered by Mexico's August 1982 default severely impacted Ecuador, drying up international credit and forcing a painful IMF structural adjustment agreement with fiscal austerity, currency devaluation, and subsidy cuts. Severe El Niño floods compounded the crisis by destroying banana and rice crops and displacing hundreds of thousands.

title: Texaco Amazon Contamination Draws Domestic and International Attention
description: Reports of widespread oil contamination from Texaco's operations in the Lago Agrio region began attracting serious domestic and international scrutiny, with contamination affecting indigenous communities and ecosystems across hundreds of thousands of hectares. The environmental damage would later be the subject of a landmark $9.5 billion lawsuit.

title: Febres-Cordero Wins Presidency; Neoliberal Reforms Launched
description: Conservative businessman León Febres-Cordero won the presidency on a pro-market platform, moving rapidly to liberalize trade, deregulate the economy, and attract foreign investment while clashing repeatedly with a hostile Congress. The Alfaro Vive Carajo guerrilla group emerged concurrently, conducting kidnappings and bank robberies and provoking harsh security responses.

title: Oil Price Collapse Devastates Ecuador's Economy; President Briefly Kidnapped
description: Global oil prices plummeted in 1986, cutting Ecuador's export revenues by half and triggering a severe fiscal crisis that demonstrated the extreme fragility of commodity dependence. President Febres-Cordero was briefly taken hostage by air force paratroopers loyal to a jailed general in an extraordinary incident that tested democratic institutions.

title: Major Earthquake Destroys SOTE Pipeline; Ecuador Suspends Debt Payments
description: A 6.9-magnitude earthquake killed over 1,000 people and destroyed a large section of the trans-Andean oil pipeline, interrupting exports for months and costing nearly $800 million in lost revenues. Ecuador suspended payments on its $8.3 billion external debt — joining Latin American countries in challenging debt servicing obligations — as the intersection of natural disaster and structural weakness proved catastrophic.

title: Rodrigo Borja Wins Presidency; AVC Guerrilla Demobilized
description: Center-left Izquierda Democrática leader Rodrigo Borja won a decisive presidential election, launching a successful national literacy campaign and negotiating the peaceful demobilization of the Alfaro Vive Carajo guerrilla organization. His administration maintained IMF-mandated austerity despite strikes while achieving Ecuador's fastest poverty literacy reduction in decades.

title: CONAIE Founded as National Indigenous Organization
description: The Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE) was formally constituted as an umbrella organization representing Ecuador's diverse indigenous peoples, rapidly becoming the most powerful indigenous movement in Latin America. CONAIE's formation laid the organizational groundwork for the transformative 1990 national uprising.

title: First National Indigenous Uprising (Levantamiento Indígena)
description: CONAIE organized Ecuador's first nationwide indigenous uprising in June 1990, paralyzing the Sierra with road blockades and demands for land rights, bilingual education, and recognition of the plurinational state. The uprising shocked the country, transformed indigenous peoples into a major political force, and set a blueprint for subsequent mobilizations.

title: Texaco Lawsuit Filed in New York Courts
description: Indigenous and settler communities from Ecuador's Amazon filed a landmark class-action lawsuit in New York federal courts against Texaco for environmental contamination affecting hundreds of thousands of hectares. The case — which involved over 30 billion gallons of toxic waste dumped between 1972 and 1993 — would evolve into the largest environmental judgment in history.

title: Amazon Indigenous Land Titling March; Ecuador Exits OPEC
description: Thousands of Amazonian indigenous people completed a historic march from Puyo to Quito, forcing the government to title over one million hectares of Amazonian land to indigenous communities in the first major territorial recognition. Ecuador simultaneously withdrew again from OPEC, citing quota restrictions that conflicted with its need to maximize oil revenues.

title: Durán Ballén Privatization Program and Financial Liberalization
description: President Sixto Durán Ballén launched a sweeping privatization agenda targeting telephone and electricity state enterprises while deregulating the financial sector by removing interest rate ceilings and easing bank licensing. The financial liberalization contributed to rapid credit expansion but sowed seeds of the catastrophic 1998–1999 banking crisis.

title: Second Indigenous Uprising Over Land Law; Vice President Dahik Corruption Scandal
description: CONAIE led a second major national uprising against the Durán Ballén government's agrarian development law, which threatened to reverse land reform gains, forcing legislative modifications. Vice President Alberto Dahik fled to Costa Rica to avoid prosecution over secret reserve fund payments in one of Ecuador's most damaging corruption affairs.

title: Cenepa War with Peru
description: Ecuador and Peru fought a brief but intense border war in the Cenepa Valley from January to March 1995 — the last armed interstate conflict in South America — with over 400 troops dying in the fighting. Ecuadorian forces performed surprisingly well, generating domestic nationalist pride, and a ceasefire brokered by Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and the United States set the stage for the 1998 peace agreement.

title: Abdalá Bucaram Elected President; Implements Austerity Despite Populism
description: Populist Abdalá Bucaram won the presidential election but then implemented IMF-friendly austerity measures and dramatic utility tariff hikes that enraged his core supporters. The Galápagos Special Law was also enacted this year, restricting immigration to the islands and strengthening conservation enforcement.

title: Bucaram Removed; Mass Protests and First Female President
description: A 48-hour general strike involving millions of Ecuadorians precipitated Congress removing President Bucaram on grounds of 'mental incapacity' in February 1997, with Vice President Rosalía Arteaga serving days as Ecuador's first female president before Congressional speaker Fabián Alarcón was named interim president. The episode demonstrated civil society's power to remove unpopular governments via mass mobilization.

title: Brasília Peace Agreement Permanently Resolves Ecuador-Peru Border Dispute
description: Ecuador and Peru signed the historic Brasília Peace Agreement on October 26, 1998, permanently resolving their 57-year Amazon border dispute and ending the longest-running territorial conflict in South American history. The treaty addressed border demarcation, commerce, waterway navigation, and confidence-building measures, ratified without opposition by both congresses.

title: Banking Crisis Erupts; 1998 Constitution Adopted
description: Ecuador's banking sector entered full crisis as massive fraud and mismanagement in institutions like Filanbanco required emergency state support, beginning a collapse that would wipe out household savings across the country. A constituent assembly simultaneously produced the 1998 constitution, including significant protections for indigenous rights, environmental rights, and collective rights.

title: Total Economic and Financial Collapse; Mass Emigration Wave
description: Ecuador experienced total economic collapse — GDP contracted by 7%, the sucre lost over 65% of its value, and a week-long bank holiday froze all deposits as multiple banks failed simultaneously, wiping out household savings. Hundreds of thousands of Ecuadorians emigrated to Spain, Italy, and the United States, creating diaspora communities that would later send billions in annual remittances.

title: Military-Indigenous Coup Ousts Mahuad; Ecuador Adopts the US Dollar
description: A CONAIE-military coalition briefly seized power from President Mahuad in January 2000 before the military high command installed Vice President Gustavo Noboa, who completed the full dollarization of the economy at 25,000 sucres per dollar. Dollarization eliminated currency risk, halted hyperinflation, and provided a stable macroeconomic anchor that survived eight successive governments.

title: OCP Heavy Crude Pipeline Construction Begins
description: Construction began on the Oleoducto de Crudos Pesados (OCP), a private heavy crude pipeline parallel to the SOTE that, upon completion in 2003, more than doubled Ecuador's oil export capacity. The project enabled exploitation of heavier Amazonian reserves and significantly increased foreign exchange earnings.

title: Lucio Gutiérrez Elected President with Indigenous Support
description: Former military officer Lucio Gutiérrez won the presidential election with support from CONAIE and Pachakutik, raising hopes for progressive governance that were quickly disappointed when he abandoned his anti-establishment platform and signed a new IMF austerity agreement in 2003. The Texaco environmental case was also definitively transferred to Ecuador's Lago Agrio court this year.

title: Gutiérrez Ousted by 'Forajidos' Uprising; Occidental Petroleum Expelled
description: Mass urban protests in Quito — demonstrators calling themselves 'forajidos' (outlaws) — forced President Gutiérrez from power in April 2005, with Vice President Alfredo Palacio assuming power constitutionally. Palacio cancelled Occidental Petroleum's oil contract for violations and seized its Block 15 assets, asserting resource nationalism.

title: Rafael Correa Wins Presidential Election; Ecuador Exits US FTA Talks
description: Rafael Correa won the presidential election in a November runoff, pledging a 'citizens' revolution' and new constitution funded by oil revenues while breaking off free trade agreement negotiations with the United States. His election began Ecuador's most transformative political period since the 1970s oil boom.

title: Yasuni-ITT Initiative Proposed; Ecuador Joins ALBA
description: Ecuador proposed the innovative Yasuni-ITT initiative, offering to leave 860 million barrels of Amazon oil unexploited if the international community compensated Ecuador for half the forgone revenues — attracting global attention but ultimately failing to raise sufficient funding. Correa simultaneously joined Venezuela's ALBA alliance and called a successful referendum approving a constituent assembly.

title: 2008 Constitution Enshrines Rights of Nature; Ecuador Defaults on External Debt
description: Ecuadorians approved the 'Constitution of Montecristi' with nearly 64% support — the first in the world to include enforceable rights of nature (Pachamama) — while simultaneously Colombia bombed FARC leader Reyes on Ecuadorian soil, triggering a diplomatic rupture. Ecuador declared portions of its commercial debt 'illegal' and defaulted on $3.2 billion in global bonds, buying them back at a steep discount.

title: Correa Closes US Manta Air Base; Ecuador Rejoins OPEC
description: President Correa declined to renew the US lease on the Manta Air Base used for drug interdiction, asserting national sovereignty in a signature anti-imperialist act. Ecuador simultaneously rejoined OPEC for the third time to benefit from collective oil market coordination during the global financial crisis.

title: Police Uprising (30-S) Briefly Traps Correa; Social Spending Surge
description: On September 30, 2010, a national police strike over pay disputes led to Correa being briefly held at a Quito hospital before a military rescue, with the government declaring it a coup attempt. The Citizens' Revolution simultaneously expanded social spending to unprecedented levels, with poverty falling from 37% in 2006 to 28% by 2011.

title: Lago Agrio Court Issues $9.5 Billion Judgment Against Chevron
description: An Ecuadorian court issued an $18.2 billion judgment (later revised to $9.5 billion) against Chevron for Texaco's Amazon contamination — the largest environmental judgment in history — though US courts subsequently ruled it unenforceable due to fraud, leaving no compensation paid to affected communities. Correa also expelled the US Ambassador over WikiLeaks cables criticizing Ecuadorian police corruption.

title: Julian Assange Granted Asylum in Ecuador's London Embassy
description: President Correa granted WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange diplomatic asylum in Ecuador's London embassy, where he would remain for seven years in a globally visible assertion of anti-imperialist foreign policy. A controversial Communications Law restricting private media was enacted the same year, drawing condemnation from international press freedom organizations.

title: Correa Wins Third Term; Yasuni-ITT Abandoned and Amazon Drilling Authorized
description: Rafael Correa won re-election with 57% in the first round — Ecuador's largest democratic mandate — then announced the failure of the Yasuni-ITT initiative after only $13 million of the $3.6 billion target was raised, authorizing oil drilling in Yasuni National Park. The decision provoked protests from environmental groups and indigenous organizations who saw it as a constitutional violation.

title: Oil Price Decline Begins; China Financing Expands; Indigenous Mining Protests
description: Global oil prices began declining sharply from mid-2014, creating fiscal pressures on Ecuador's oil-dependent public finances while the government signed multi-billion dollar infrastructure financing agreements with Chinese state banks requiring repayment in oil. Shuar and Waorani communities staged protests against expanding large-scale mining concessions granted to Chinese companies.

title: Massive Anti-Correa Protests; Cotopaxi Volcano Reactivates
description: Hundreds of thousands of Ecuadorians took to the streets in June 2015 in the largest demonstrations of the Correa era, protesting proposed inheritance and capital gains taxes, forcing the government to withdraw the proposals. Cotopaxi volcano reactivated in August, prompting mass evacuations from potential lava flow paths and a state of emergency.

title: 7.8 Magnitude Earthquake Kills 650 in Manabí Province
description: A powerful 7.8 earthquake struck Ecuador's Pacific coast on April 16, 2016, killing over 650 people, injuring thousands, and destroying tens of thousands of homes in Manabí and Esmeraldas — the country's deadliest earthquake since 1949. International humanitarian aid and a major reconstruction program were launched amid ongoing fiscal austerity from declining oil revenues.

title: Lenin Moreno Wins Presidency; Breaks with Correa
description: Lenin Moreno narrowly won the presidential election as Correa's designated successor, but launched a national dialogue process, released political prisoners, and began distancing himself dramatically from Correa's authoritarian tendencies. The rupture between Moreno and Correa — culminating in Correa being charged with bribery linked to the Odebrecht scandal in 2018 — became the defining political drama of the period.

title: Three Journalists Kidnapped and Killed Near Colombian Border
description: Three Ecuadorian journalists were kidnapped and murdered near the Colombian border by a dissident FARC faction, shocking the country and highlighting the violent spillover of Colombian organized crime. The killings prompted emergency security measures along the northern border and foreshadowed Ecuador's own narco-violence surge.

title: October Uprising Against Fuel Subsidy Cuts Forces Government Reversal
description: The elimination of fuel subsidies demanded by a $4.2 billion IMF deal triggered an 11-day national uprising in October 2019, with CONAIE leading protests that paralyzed Quito and forced the government to temporarily relocate to Guayaquil — killing 8, injuring 1,340, and detaining 1,192. President Moreno reversed the fuel subsidy elimination under a televised agreement with CONAIE leaders.

title: COVID-19 Overwhelms Guayaquil; Economy Contracts 7.8%
description: Ecuador, particularly Guayaquil, became one of the first Latin American cities overwhelmed by COVID-19, with bodies left in streets due to collapsed funeral and hospital systems in scenes broadcast worldwide. GDP contracted approximately 7.8% — among the worst in Latin America — from the combined impact of the pandemic, low oil prices, and austerity.

title: Guillermo Lasso Wins Presidency; Prison Massacres Expose Gang Penetration
description: Conservative banker Guillermo Lasso defeated CONAIE-backed Yaku Pérez in a close runoff, becoming Ecuador's first center-right president in over a decade and ending 14 years of Citizens' Revolution governance. Ecuador's prison system erupted in violence in February, with over 80 inmates killed in a single day as drug gang rivalries turned penitentiaries into killing fields.

title: 18-Day Indigenous Uprising Forces 218-Point Agreement; Organized Crime Escalates
description: CONAIE led an 18-day national uprising in June 2022 demanding fuel price reductions and protection of indigenous territories, shutting down major highways until the Lasso government agreed to a comprehensive 218-point negotiated agreement. Ecuador's homicide rate nearly quadrupled between 2019 and 2022 as drug trafficking gangs — particularly Los Lobos and the Águilas — spread violence across cities and prisons.

title: Lasso Invokes 'Muerte Cruzada'; Villavicencio Assassinated; Noboa Elected
description: President Lasso invoked the unprecedented 'muerte cruzada' constitutional mechanism to dissolve the National Assembly and call snap elections rather than face an impeachment vote, triggering a constitutional first in Latin America. Anti-corruption presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio was assassinated at a campaign rally in August; 35-year-old Daniel Noboa subsequently won the election pledging a hard-line approach to criminal violence.

title: Historic Referendum Votes to Halt Yasuni Amazon Oil Drilling
description: Nearly 60% of Ecuadorians voted in a landmark August 2023 referendum to halt oil extraction in the ITT block of Yasuni National Park — the first time citizens anywhere in the world voted to leave oil reserves unexploited — protecting 1.67 billion barrels and the territories of voluntarily isolated indigenous peoples. The result required the state to wind down operations within one year.

title: TC Televisión Siege; Noboa Declares Internal Armed Conflict
description: Armed men from Los Choneros gang seized a live TC Televisión broadcast in Guayaquil in January 2024, pointing weapons at journalists on air, moments after gang leader 'Fito' disappeared from prison — triggering President Noboa to declare Ecuador in a state of 'internal armed conflict' and designate 22 criminal organizations as terrorist groups. Ecuador's homicide rate had risen from 6.7 per 100,000 in 2019 to an estimated 45 per 100,000 by 2023.

title: Ecuador Invades Mexican Embassy to Arrest Former Vice President Glas
description: Ecuadorian police stormed the Mexican embassy in Quito to arrest former Vice President Jorge Glas — who had been granted asylum by Mexico — in a violation of international diplomatic law condemned across Latin America and by the United Nations. Mexico broke diplomatic relations with Ecuador as a result.

title: Noboa Re-elected in Landslide; Energy Crisis Hits Nationwide
description: Daniel Noboa won re-election in the first round in October 2024 with approximately 84% of the vote — Ecuador's most decisive electoral mandate in decades — driven by strong security-focused leadership. Ecuador simultaneously experienced severe electricity rationing with daily cuts of up to 14 hours due to drought affecting hydropower reservoirs, revealing dangerous dependence on hydroelectric generation.

title: NEE-01 Pegaso Becomes Ecuador's First Satellite in Orbit
description: Ecuador's first satellite, the CubeSat NEE-01 Pegaso, built by the Ecuadorian Civilian Space Agency (EXA) for about $30,000, launched as a secondary payload on a Chinese Long March 2D rocket on 26 April 2013. It transmitted the first live video from orbit on 16 May 2013 before a close pass with rocket debris on 23 May 2013 damaged it; a 2014 signal recovery later confirmed it had survived the collision.

title: Quito Named UNESCO's First World Heritage City
description: On September 18, 1978, the historic center of Quito was inscribed by UNESCO alongside Krakow, Poland, becoming one of the first World Heritage Sites ever declared and the first historic city center recognized under the new convention. The designation cited Quito's dense concentration of 16th-18th century colonial architecture and its living indigenous and Spanish colonial traditions, among the best-preserved historic centers in Latin America. The listing helped drive decades of subsequent restoration investment in Quito's old town.
